subject: Mathematics
chapter_title: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:

Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangles with these sidelengths (all in cm) using compass and ruler: (a) 4, 4, 6; (b) 3, 4, 5; (c) 1, 5, 5; (d) 4, 6, 8; (e) 3.5, 3.5, 3.5.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.1 p.150
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use points on a circle and/or its centre to form isosceles triangles (diagram given with one circle).

periods.activity_title: Building Equilateral Triangles with Compass and Ruler

time_bands.activity: Open with the question: how would you place a third point so it is equally far from both ends of a 4 cm base? Invite students to mark guesses on paper, then reveal that arcs drawn from each endpoint at the same radius solve this precisely — the arc idea from their Grade 6 experience of finding equidistant points.

Students work through Construct, section 7.1 p.150 ("Construct triangles with these sidelengths (all in cm) using compass and ruler....") in pairs: draw a base, swing matching arcs from each end, mark the intersection C, join the sides. Encourage students to notice that C lies on both arcs and hence both new sides equal the chosen radius.

Groups tackle Figure it Out Q1, section 7.1 p.150 ("Use points on a circle and/or its centre to form isosceles triangles...."). Students identify which vertex positions guarantee equal sides by reasoning about radii, then share one observation with the class.

Class discussion: students articulate why two arcs of the same radius from two endpoints always produce a triangle with two equal sides. Teacher highlights the key insight — the arc radius IS the side length — and consolidates the three-step construction sequence.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who swing arcs of different radii for each endpoint when constructing the equilateral case — a quiet error that produces an isosceles triangle instead. Prompt: 'What does the radius of each arc represent about that side?' Figure it Out Q2, section 7.1 p.150 extends the circle-point reasoning to three equal circles and is a strong self-study companion for confident learners.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.1 p.150
homework.description: Use points on two (or three) equal circles and/or their centres A, B (and C) to form isosceles and equilateral triangles.

textbook_segments.title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given

textbook_items_in_class.description: Attempt to construct triangles with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm and 2 cm, 3 cm, 6 cm. Find more sets of lengths for which a triangle is impossible, and identify a pattern.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.154
textbook_items_in_class.description: Without constructing: could you have determined that 3, 4, 8 cm and 2, 3, 6 cm cannot form triangles? Explain using the triangle inequality.

periods.activity_title: When Do Three Lengths Make a Triangle?

time_bands.activity: Students attempt Math Talk, section 7.2 p.151 ("Attempt to construct triangles with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm and 2 cm, 3 cm, 6 cm....") using compass and ruler. The expectation is that the arcs do not intersect; students observe this directly and record what they see happening on the page.

Pairs generate their own impossible triplets and look for a pattern. Teacher introduces the tent-tree-pole path metaphor: the direct path is always shorter than the two-leg detour, making the key relationship emerge from concrete reasoning rather than statement alone.

Class unpacks Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.154 ("Without constructing: could you have determined that 3, 4, 8 cm cannot form triangles? Explain...."). Students articulate the triangle inequality in their own words: each side must be less than the sum of the other two.

Teacher draws the circle-intersection diagram on the board (circles touch, don't meet, intersect in two points) and connects each picture to a numerical case. Students state whether their own generated triplets match the 'no intersection' picture and explain why.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is checking only one inequality — for example, confirming only that the longest side is less than the sum of the two shorter sides and stopping there. While that single check is sufficient (the other two inequalities follow automatically when the longest side passes), students should understand WHY, not just apply a shortcut without reasoning. Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.154 makes a good independent check set and is recommended as self-study for students who complete early.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.154
homework.description: Determine whether triangles exist for: (a) 10 km, 10 km, 25 km; (b) 5 mm, 10 mm, 20 mm; (c) 12 cm, 20 cm, 40 cm.

textbook_segments.title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.156
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which sets of lengths can be sidelengths of a triangle? Explain: (a) 2, 2, 5; (b) 3, 4, 6; (c) 2, 4, 8; (d) 5, 5, 8; (e) 10, 20, 25; (f) 10, 20, 35; (g) 24, 26, 28.
For each pair of given sides, find at least 5 valid values for the third side: (a) 1, 100; (b) 5, 5; (c) 3, 7. Describe all possible third-side values for each case.

periods.activity_title: Applying the Triangle Inequality: Construct and Check

time_bands.activity: Quick mental warm-up: teacher reads out three lengths (e.g., 6, 9, 14) and students hold up a thumb up or down before any working. Collect a sample of predictions, then establish the habit of applying the triangle inequality as the decision rule.

Students work independently on Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.156 ("Which sets of lengths can be sidelengths of a triangle? Explain: (a) 2, 2, 5; (b) 3, 4, 6...."). For each case they write a one-line justification referencing the inequality, not just a yes/no answer.

Try This Q3, section 7.2 p.159 ("For each pair of given sides, find at least 5 valid values for the third side: (a) 1, 100; (b) 5, 5; (c) 3, 7....") is tackled in pairs. Students record their values and describe the range in words: 'the third side must be greater than ___ and less than ___'.

Whole-class share: one pair presents their range for case (a) 1, 100. Teacher formalises the boundary: third side lies strictly between |a − b| and a + b, connecting the students' list of valid values to the inequality's two-sided constraint.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established through experimentation that arcs fail to intersect when the triangle inequality is violated, students are now formalising that reasoning into a procedure. Watch for students who accept the boundary values (e.g., the third side exactly equalling the sum) as valid — prompt them to ask what the triangle would look like in that degenerate case. Try This Q3, section 7.2 p.159 is rich and time-intensive; groups that move quickly can explore case (c) 3, 7 in detail.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.159
homework.description: Check if a triangle exists for: (a) 1, 100, 100; (b) 3, 6, 9; (c) 1, 1, 5; (d) 5, 10, 12.

textbook_segments.title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given

textbook_items_in_class.description: Find 3 examples each of sidelength sets where the two circles: (a) touch each other at a point; (b) do not intersect. Frame a complete procedure to check the existence of a triangle.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.159
textbook_items_in_class.description: Does an equilateral triangle exist with sides 50, 50, 50? In general, does an equilateral triangle of any sidelength exist? Justify.

periods.activity_title: Framing the Existence Procedure: Circle-Intersection Cases

time_bands.activity: Teacher recalls the circle-intersection diagram (circles touch, don't meet, intersect at two points) and asks students to predict, for each case, what the triangle inequality says about the three side lengths. Students state their predictions before any computation.

Students work on Figure it Out, section 7.2 p.158 ("Find 3 examples each of sidelength sets where the two circles: (a) touch each other at a point; (b) do not intersect. Frame a complete procedure to check the existence of a triangle...."). They construct or calculate examples for each circle-pair type and write a step-by-step existence-check procedure in their own words.

Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.159 ("Does an equilateral triangle exist with sides 50, 50, 50? In general, does an equilateral triangle of any sidelength exist? Justify...."). Students apply their procedure to confirm equilateral triangles always pass the inequality, then generalise: for three equal sides s, each comparison gives s < 2s, which is always true.

Groups share their written existence-check procedures. Teacher highlights any that are complete and algorithmic, noting the parallel with a recipe: given three lengths, apply the comparison, interpret the result. The class agrees on a shared concise form.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit deepens the triangle-inequality work by asking students to move from applying the rule to articulating it as a self-contained procedure — an algorithmic thinking task. Watch for procedures that only check 'largest side < sum of other two' without explaining why that single check suffices; the richest procedures will note that the other two inequalities follow automatically when all sides are positive. Try This Q3, section 7.2 p.154 is assigned as a reflective extension on which comparison is always the binding one.

homework.description: For any set of three lengths, will at least two comparisons always satisfy 'direct length < sum of other two'? Explore. Also find which length can be identified as immediately less than the sum without calculation.

textbook_segments.title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.161
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangles given two sides and the included angle: (a) 3 cm, 75°, 7 cm; (b) 6 cm, 25°, 3 cm; (c) 3 cm, 120°, 8 cm.
Is there a combination of two sides and an included angle for which a triangle is not possible? Justify from your construction observations.

periods.activity_title: Two Sides and an Included Angle: When Does a Triangle Exist?

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates the four-step SAS construction on the board: draw base, construct the given angle at one endpoint, mark the second given length along the angle arm, join to close the triangle. Students narrate each step aloud as it is drawn.

Students construct all three cases in Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.161 ("Construct triangles given two sides and the included angle: (a) 3 cm, 75°, 7 cm; (b) 6 cm, 25°, 3 cm; (c) 3 cm, 120°, 8 cm...."). They annotate each figure with the included angle and check that both given sides are correctly placed.

Math Talk, section 7.3 p.161 ("Is there a combination of two sides and an included angle for which a triangle is not possible?...."). Students test extreme angles — very close to 0° and at 180° — and report what they observe geometrically. The class gathers evidence that only an angle of 180° or more prevents triangle formation.

Brief consolidation: class states the existence condition for SAS in one sentence. Teacher notes the contrast with the three-side case — here the existence condition is almost always satisfied unless the angle is degenerate.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes place the protractor at the wrong endpoint or construct the angle from the wrong side, producing a reflection of the intended triangle. Encourage them to label both given sides before marking the angle so the 'included' position is explicit. Math Talk, section 7.3 p.161 is designed to surface the degenerate angle boundary rather than merely confirm that most angles work.

textbook_segments.title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.162
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangles given two angles and the included side: (a) 75°, 5 cm, 75°; (b) 25°, 3 cm, 60°; (c) 120°, 6 cm, 30°.
Do triangles always exist for every combination of two angles and the included side? Find examples where they do not.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.165
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the third angle (using a parallel-line argument) when two angles are: (a) 36°, 72°; (b) 150°, 15°; (c) 90°, 30°; (d) 75°, 45°.

periods.activity_title: Two Angles and the Included Side: Parallelism and the Angle-Sum Proof

time_bands.activity: Students construct the three ASA cases in Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.162 ("Construct triangles given two angles and the included side: (a) 75°, 5 cm, 75°; (b) 25°, 3 cm, 60°; (c) 120°, 6 cm, 30°...."). They observe whether and where the two angle arms meet and record any surprises.

Math Talk, section 7.3 p.162 ("Do triangles always exist for every combination of two angles and the included side? Find examples where they do not...."). Students test pairs summing to 180° and beyond, discover that parallel arms never meet, and articulate the condition: angle pair sum must be less than 180°.

Teacher presents the parallel-line proof of the angle-sum property: draw XY ∥ BC through A, identify alternate interior angles ∠XAB = ∠B and ∠YAC = ∠C, and observe that the three angles form a straight angle at A. Students then apply the result to Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.165 ("Find the third angle using a parallel-line argument when two angles are: (a) 36°, 72°....").

Students state the angle-sum property in their own words and identify what makes the parallel-line construction work as a proof. Teacher connects: the same reasoning that explains why two supplementary base angles produce parallel arms also underpins the straight-angle argument at A.

periods.teacher_notes: Having proved that alternate angles on a parallel line are equal, the step from construction failure to a formal proof of the angle sum is a short deductive move — make this link explicit on the board. Watch for students who confuse the alternate interior angles with corresponding angles; a quick diagram showing both pair types helps. Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.163 extends the angle-pair reasoning and is assigned as reinforcement.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.163
homework.description: For each given angle (a) 30°; (b) 70°; (c) 54°; (d) 144°, find at least two angles for which a triangle is possible and two for which it is not. Find the third angle in each valid case.

textbook_segments.title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.163
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine which angle pairs can be two angles of a triangle: (a) 35°, 150°; (b) 70°, 30°; (c) 90°, 85°; (d) 50°, 150°.

Exterior angle: find ∠ACD if ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°. Then find the exterior angle for different ∠A and ∠B values and derive the relationship between the exterior angle and the two non-adjacent interior angles.

periods.activity_title: Angle Conditions, Exterior Angles, and Triangle Existence

time_bands.activity: Students tackle Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.163 ("Determine which angle pairs can be two angles of a triangle: (a) 35°, 150°; (b) 70°, 30°; (c) 90°, 85°; (d) 50°, 150°...."). For each valid pair, they find the third angle using the angle-sum property; for each invalid pair, they state which constraint is violated.

Figure it Out, section 7.3 p.166 ("Exterior angle: find ∠ACD if ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°. Then find exterior angles for different ∠A and ∠B values and derive the relationship...."). Students tabulate several (∠A, ∠B, exterior angle) triples, notice the pattern, then justify it: exterior angle = 180° − ∠C = ∠A + ∠B, because ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°.

A short group challenge: students create two angle pairs — one that forms a valid triangle and one that does not — and swap with another group to identify which is which. This extends the existence reasoning to a peer-authored context.

Whole-class close: the exterior-angle relationship is stated formally. Teacher invites students to explain it using the angle-sum property in one sentence, grounding the derivation rather than leaving it as a memorised formula.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often compute the exterior angle as 180° minus the adjacent interior angle only, forgetting that this equals the sum of the two non-adjacent angles — remind them the two derivations are equivalent and that the second form is more useful for problem-solving. Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.165 (equal-angle and equilateral cases) is a natural self-study extension for students who want to test the angle-sum property in symmetric situations.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.165
homework.description: Can a triangle have all three angles equal to 70°? If two angles are 70°, what is the third? If all angles are equal, what must each be?

textbook_segments.title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given

textbook_items_in_class.description: Experiment with different triangles to find a relation between any two angles and the third. What data will you track and how will you organise it?
In triangle ABC, ∠B = ∠C and ∠A = 50°. Find ∠B and ∠C.

periods.activity_title: Angle Exploration: Third Angles and Impossible Pairs

time_bands.activity: Students draw three different triangles of their own choice, measure all three angles with a protractor, and record the triples in a table. Teacher prompts: 'What do you notice about the three numbers in each row?'

Math Talk, section 7.3 p.164 ("Experiment with different triangles to find a relation between any two angles and the third. What data will you track and how will you organise it?...."). Groups compare tables across the class, agree on the pattern, and write a conjecture in their own words before the teacher confirms the angle-sum result.

Try This Q3, section 7.3 p.165 ("In triangle ABC, ∠B = ∠C and ∠A = 50°. Find ∠B and ∠C...."). Students apply the angle-sum property to an isosceles-angle scenario, practising algebraic use of the rule: ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°, and ∠B = ∠C, so 50° + 2∠B = 180°.

Wrap-up: students pose one impossible angle pair of their own and explain to a partner why it fails. Teacher listens in and selects one clear and one subtle example to briefly discuss with the whole class.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit deepens the angle-sum property through independent data collection rather than teacher demonstration, building the habit of using organised tables to extract a conjecture. A typical error is summing angles to 181° or 179° due to protractor misreading — encourage students to accept measurements within 2° of 180° as confirming the property rather than disproving it. Try This Q3, section 7.3 p.165 rewards the student who can write an equation and solve it, a good differentiating task.

textbook_segments.title: Constructions Related to Altitudes of Triangles

textbook_items_in_class.description: Altitudes Using Paper Folding: cut out a paper triangle, fix one side as the base, and fold so the crease is the altitude from the top vertex to the base. Justify why the crease is perpendicular to the base.
Visualise and draw a rough diagram: in what type of triangle is a side also an altitude?
Construct the altitude from A to BC using ruler and set square, for the given triangle (extended base case shown also).

periods.activity_title: Finding the Altitude: Paper Folding and Set-Square Methods

time_bands.activity: Each student cuts out a paper triangle and performs Activity, section 7.4 p.168 ("Altitudes Using Paper Folding: cut out a paper triangle, fix one side as the base, and fold so the crease is the altitude from the top vertex...."). They mark where the crease meets the base and explain in a sentence why folding makes the crease perpendicular — the fold matches the two halves exactly, so the angle cannot be anything but 90°.

Figure it Out, section 7.4 p.168 ("Visualise and draw a rough diagram: in what type of triangle is a side also an altitude?...."). Students sketch the right-angled triangle case and annotate which side serves as the altitude to which base, grounding the definition of a right angle within the construction context.

Teacher demonstrates the set-square-and-ruler method: align the ruler to the base, place the set square so its right angle touches the ruler's edge, slide until the vertical edge reaches the chosen vertex, draw the altitude. Students replicate this for Figure it Out, section 7.4 p.169 ("Construct the altitude from A to BC using ruler and set square...."), including the extended base case.

Students compare the paper-folding crease with the set-square altitude drawn on the same triangle and confirm they coincide. Teacher consolidates the definition: the altitude is the perpendicular segment from a vertex to the line of the opposite side.

periods.teacher_notes: The paper-folding step often produces a crease that misses the vertex if the fold is careless — remind students that one end of the crease must land exactly on the top vertex, and the other on the base (or its extension). For obtuse triangles the altitude falls outside the triangle; Figure it Out, section 7.4 p.169 includes this case, which surprises many students and is worth discussing.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.5 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangle ABC with BC = 5 cm, AB = 6 cm, CA = 5 cm. Construct the altitude from A to BC.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 7.5 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: Through construction, explore whether it is possible to construct: (a) a right-angled equilateral triangle; (b) an obtuse-angled equilateral triangle; (c) a right-angled isosceles triangle; (d) an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle.

periods.activity_title: Sorting Triangles: Sides, Angles, and Their Names

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the six triangle names on the board (equilateral, isosceles, scalene by sides; acute-angled, right-angled, obtuse-angled by angles) and invites students to recall definitions in their own words before any formal statement is given. A quick class sort: teacher reads out a triangle description and students classify it by both side-type and angle-type simultaneously.

Students construct Figure it Out Q1, section 7.5 p.170 ("Construct triangle ABC with BC = 5 cm, AB = 6 cm, CA = 5 cm. Construct the altitude from A to BC....") and label the triangle by both side and angle type. The altitude from A is added using the set-square method, reinforcing the construction technique from the altitude work on perpendicular distance.

Figure it Out Q4, section 7.5 p.170 ("Through construction, explore whether it is possible to construct: (a) a right-angled equilateral triangle; (b) an obtuse-angled equilateral triangle; (c) a right-angled isosceles triangle; (d) an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle...."). Students attempt each by construction and angle-sum reasoning, noting that equilateral means each angle is 60° so it cannot be right-angled or obtuse.

Class discussion: which combinations of the two classification systems are possible, which are impossible, and why the angle-sum property settles each impossible case. Teacher notes that the full relationship between the two systems is explored further in a later chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes believe every isosceles triangle must be acute — Figure it Out Q4, section 7.5 p.170 is designed to correct this by having them construct an obtuse isosceles triangle themselves. Watch also for confusion between 'right-angled' as a type-by-angle and a side being an altitude — the paper-folding and altitude work from the altitude unit grounds the right-angle concept geometrically rather than leaving it as a label. Figure it Out Q2, section 7.5 p.170 is assigned as a paired altitude-construction exercise.

homework.description: Construct triangle TRY with RY = 4 cm, TR = 7 cm, ∠R = 140°. Construct the altitude from T to RY.

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis: Constructing, Classifying, and Proving

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses a rapid-fire verbal review: 'Name one condition that makes three lengths fail the triangle inequality'; 'State the angle-sum property in one sentence'; 'Name a triangle type by sides and one by angles'. Students respond in pairs, warming up all five sections' ideas without recapping any single unit.

Groups receive a combined construction task: given three measurements (two sides and an included angle), construct the triangle, classify it by both sides and angles using the equilateral-isosceles-scalene and acute-right-obtuse frameworks, construct one altitude, and state the exterior-angle sum at that vertex. Figure it Out, section 7.3 p.166 ("Exterior angle: find ∠ACD if ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°....") guides the exterior-angle component.

Figure it Out Q4, section 7.5 p.170 ("Through construction, explore whether it is possible to construct: (a) a right-angled equilateral triangle; (b) an obtuse-angled equilateral triangle; (c) a right-angled isosceles triangle; (d) an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle....") is revisited as a synthesis question: students must now use the angle-sum property (60° per angle in equilateral) and triangle-inequality reasoning together to explain each impossible case, not just construct or reject by trial.

Whole-class close: each group contributes one sentence connecting two ideas from different sections of the chapter — for example, 'the triangle-inequality failure corresponds to circles not intersecting' or 'the angle-sum property explains why a right-angled equilateral triangle is impossible'. Teacher weaves the contributions into a spoken map of the chapter's core ideas.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit deliberately does not assume any prior activity, worksheet, or discussion from earlier units: the tasks are self-contained and solvable from content alone. The exterior-angle and classification-combination problems work well for confident students; the verbal review opening ensures students who met this content through different routes can participate fully. Watch for students who correctly classify a triangle by sides but misclassify by angles — the angle-sum property resolves any ambiguity and is the canonical check.

items.section_title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given
items.prompt: Three lengths are given: 4 cm, 5 cm, and 11 cm. Explain, without constructing, whether these lengths can form a triangle. Use the triangle inequality in your explanation.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No triangle is possible. The triangle inequality requires each side to be less than the sum of the other two. Checking the longest side: 11 must be less than 4 + 5 = 9, but 11 > 9, so the inequality is violated and no triangle exists.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether the longest side is less than the sum of the other two sides; here 11 > 4 + 5 = 9, so the triangle inequality fails.

inclusivity.support: Pair with a classmate to say aloud what 4 + 5 equals, then compare that sum with 11 before writing.
inclusivity.challenge: If the longest side is changed to 8 cm (keeping 4 cm and 5 cm), does a triangle become possible? Justify, and then find the complete range of values the third side could take.

exercise.description: Attempt to construct triangles with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm and 2 cm, 3 cm, 6 cm. Find more sets of lengths for which a triangle is impossible, and identify a pattern.

items.section_title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given
items.prompt: Two sides of a triangle are 5 cm and 8 cm, and the angle between them is 175°. Explain whether a triangle can be formed with these measurements. What happens geometrically when the included angle approaches 180°?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A triangle cannot be formed when the included angle is 180° because the three points become collinear — the two sides lie along the same straight line. At 175° the angle arm is nearly straight and the third side is very short; as the included angle reaches 180°, the two endpoints of the given sides coincide on a line and no enclosed figure exists. For any included angle strictly less than 180° a triangle can be formed, so 175° technically does produce a (very flat) triangle, but the limiting case at 180° does not.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Reason from the SAS construction: the included angle determines how open the two sides are; at 180° they are collinear and the vertex C coincides with a point on the base line.

inclusivity.support: Talk through the construction steps with a partner before writing: draw the base, construct the angle at one endpoint, mark the second side — what does 'almost 180°' look like on paper?
inclusivity.challenge: Change the condition: what if the included angle is exactly 0°? Describe what happens geometrically and whether a triangle exists in that limiting case.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.161
exercise.description: Construct triangles given two sides and the included angle: (a) 3 cm, 75°, 7 cm; (b) 6 cm, 25°, 3 cm; (c) 3 cm, 120°, 8 cm.

items.section_title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given
items.prompt: In triangle PQR, a line XY is drawn through P parallel to QR. Explain how this construction proves that the sum of the angles of any triangle is 180°. Name each pair of equal angles you use and state the geometric reason for their equality.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Draw XY through P with XY ∥ QR. Angle XPQ equals angle Q because they are alternate interior angles formed by transversal PQ cutting the parallel lines XY and QR. Angle YPR equals angle R because they are alternate interior angles formed by transversal PR cutting the same pair of parallel lines. The three angles at P — angle XPQ, angle QPR, and angle YPR — together make a straight angle (180°) along line XY. Substituting: angle Q + angle QPR + angle R = 180°, which is the angle-sum property.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw XY ∥ QR through P, identify two pairs of alternate interior angles, and observe that the three angles at P form a straight angle.

inclusivity.support: Before writing, sketch the diagram and label the angles at P as three separate parts of the straight line, then match each part to an angle in the triangle.
inclusivity.challenge: Use the same parallel-line argument to derive the exterior-angle theorem: show that an exterior angle of the triangle equals the sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.162
exercise.description: Construct triangles given two angles and the included side: (a) 75°, 5 cm, 75°; (b) 25°, 3 cm, 60°; (c) 120°, 6 cm, 30°.

items.prompt: A compass is set to a radius of 6 cm. A student draws a base segment AB of length 6 cm, then swings one arc of radius 6 cm centred at A and another arc of radius 6 cm centred at B. The arcs meet at point C. Without measuring, state the lengths of AC and BC, and explain why each equals 6 cm.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: AC = 6 cm and BC = 6 cm. C lies on the arc centred at A with radius 6 cm, so by definition the distance from A to C equals 6 cm. C also lies on the arc centred at B with radius 6 cm, so the distance from B to C equals 6 cm. Because AB = AC = BC = 6 cm, triangle ABC is equilateral.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the definition of a circle/arc: every point on an arc is exactly one radius-length from the centre.

inclusivity.support: Refer to the definition of an arc in section 7.1 of your textbook — every point on the arc is the same distance from the centre as the radius.
inclusivity.challenge: If the compass is reset to 4 cm for one arc and kept at 6 cm for the other, what kind of triangle is formed? Name it by sides and explain.

exercise.description: Construct triangles with these sidelengths (all in cm) using compass and ruler: (a) 4, 4, 6; (b) 3, 4, 5; (c) 1, 5, 5; (d) 4, 6, 8; (e) 3.5, 3.5, 3.5.

items.section_title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given
items.prompt:
For each set of three lengths below, state whether a triangle can be formed. Show the key inequality check for each case.
(a) 7, 9, 15
(b) 6, 6, 6
(c) 3, 8, 12

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) 7 + 9 = 16 > 15, so a triangle is possible. (b) 6 + 6 = 12 > 6, so a triangle is possible (equilateral). (c) 3 + 8 = 11 < 12, so no triangle is possible — the longest side exceeds the sum of the other two.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether the longest side is strictly less than the sum of the other two sides using the triangle inequality.

inclusivity.support: Draw a number line and mark the sum of the two shorter sides, then compare that sum to the longest side to make the comparison visual.
inclusivity.challenge: For case (a), find the complete range of values that the third side could take if only the two shorter sides (7 and 9) were given, and state the range as an inequality.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.156
exercise.description: Which sets of lengths can be sidelengths of a triangle? Explain: (a) 2, 2, 5; (b) 3, 4, 6; (c) 2, 4, 8; (d) 5, 5, 8; (e) 10, 20, 25; (f) 10, 20, 35; (g) 24, 26, 28.

items.section_title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given
items.prompt: Two circles are drawn: circle 1 centred at point A with radius 5 cm, and circle 2 centred at point B with radius 3 cm, where AB = 9 cm. Do the two circles intersect, touch at exactly one point, or not meet at all? Use the triangle-inequality reasoning to justify your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: For the two circles to intersect at two points, the three lengths 5, 3, and 9 (the two radii and the distance AB) must satisfy the triangle inequality. Check: 5 + 3 = 8, and 8 < 9, so the sum of the two radii is less than the distance between the centres. The circles do not intersect at all — they are too far apart. Geometrically, the circle of radius 3 centred at B lies entirely inside the gap and the two circles have no common point.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the sum of the two radii (5 + 3 = 8) with the distance between centres (9): since 8 < 9, the circles do not meet.

inclusivity.support: Draw two points A and B 9 cm apart on paper, draw rough circles of radius 5 and 3 around them, and look at whether the circles reach each other.
inclusivity.challenge: Find the exact distance AB at which the two circles of radii 5 and 3 would touch at exactly one point, and state what that distance tells you about the triangle that would be formed in that limiting case.

exercise.description: Find 3 examples each of sidelength sets where the two circles: (a) touch each other at a point; (b) do not intersect. Frame a complete procedure to check the existence of a triangle.

items.section_title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given
items.prompt: In triangle DEF, ∠D = 48° and ∠E = 93°. Find ∠F. Then find the exterior angle at vertex F (the angle formed between side EF extended beyond F and side DF). Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: ∠D + ∠E + ∠F = 180°, so 48° + 93° + ∠F = 180°, giving ∠F = 180° − 141° = 39°. The exterior angle at F is supplementary to ∠F: exterior angle = 180° − 39° = 141°. Alternatively, the exterior angle equals the sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles: 48° + 93° = 141°. Both methods give 141°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the angle-sum property to find ∠F, then use either the linear-pair supplement or the exterior-angle theorem (exterior angle = sum of two non-adjacent interior angles).

inclusivity.support: First write the angle-sum equation with a blank for ∠F, solve it, then separately write that the exterior angle and ∠F together make a straight line (180°).
inclusivity.challenge: Verify your answer using both methods (supplement and sum of non-adjacent angles) and explain in one sentence why the two methods must always give the same result.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.163
exercise.description: Determine which angle pairs can be two angles of a triangle: (a) 35°, 150°; (b) 70°, 30°; (c) 90°, 85°; (d) 50°, 150°.

items.section_title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given
items.prompt: In triangle XYZ, ∠X = 2 × ∠Z and ∠Y = 60°. Find the values of ∠X and ∠Z.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Using the angle-sum property: ∠X + ∠Y + ∠Z = 180°. Substituting ∠Y = 60° and ∠X = 2∠Z: 2∠Z + 60° + ∠Z = 180°, so 3∠Z = 120°, giving ∠Z = 40° and ∠X = 80°. Check: 80° + 60° + 40° = 180°. ✓
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Set up the angle-sum equation with ∠X expressed as 2∠Z, substitute ∠Y = 60°, and solve the resulting linear equation.

inclusivity.support: Replace ∠X with '2 × ∠Z' in the angle-sum equation before solving, and check your answer by adding all three angles.
inclusivity.challenge: Classify triangle XYZ by its angles, and explain whether a triangle with these angle measures can also be classified as isosceles.

exercise.description: Experiment with different triangles to find a relation between any two angles and the third. What data will you track and how will you organise it?

items.section_title: Constructions Related to Altitudes of Triangles
items.prompt: A student folds a paper triangle so that the fold crease passes from vertex A and lands on side BC, forming a right angle with BC at the point where it meets BC. What is the geometric name for the crease, and what property of the crease confirms it is perpendicular to BC?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The crease is the altitude from vertex A to side BC. When the paper is folded so the two halves of BC coincide exactly along the crease, the crease makes equal angles on both sides of BC; equal angles that together form a straight angle must each be 90°, confirming the crease is perpendicular to BC. This is the definition of an altitude: the perpendicular segment from a vertex to the line of the opposite side.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify that the altitude is defined as the perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side, and use the folding argument (equal angles summing to 180°) to confirm perpendicularity.

inclusivity.support: Re-read the definition of altitude in section 7.4 of your textbook, then describe what 'perpendicular' means in terms of the angle the crease makes with the base.
inclusivity.challenge: Describe what happens to the altitude when the triangle is obtuse — does the crease still land on side BC, or somewhere else? Explain.

exercise.description: Visualise and draw a rough diagram: in what type of triangle is a side also an altitude?
